claim: SPVL is highly variable in the Rakai population, with values ranging from 10² copies/mL to 10⁷ copies/mL.
source: As in other HIV epidemics, we found that SPVL is highly variable in this population, with values ranging from 102 copies/mL to 107 copies/mL.
evidence: The manuscript directly states the range of SPVL values observed in the population.

claim: SPVL was calculated for 647 HIV incident cases in the Rakai cohort.
source: SPVL was calculated for 647 individuals who had a positive HIV serologic test within two study visits of their last negative test ('HIV incident cases', Table 1; median time between last negative visit and first positive visit is 1.25 years)
evidence: The manuscript provides the specific number of incident cases for which SPVL was calculated.

claim: SPVL was calculated for 817 participants in serodiscordant partnerships in the Rakai cohort.
source: SPVL was calculated for 647 individuals who had a positive HIV serologic test within two study visits of their last negative test ('HIV incident cases', Table 1; median time between last negative visit and first positive visit is 1.25 years), and for 817 participants in a serodiscordant partnership ('serodiscordant couples', Table 2).
evidence: The manuscript provides the specific number of serodiscordant couples for which SPVL was calculated.

claim: The median time between last negative visit and first positive visit for HIV incident cases is 1.25 years.
source: SPVL was calculated for 647 individuals who had a positive HIV serologic test within two study visits of their last negative test ('HIV incident cases', Table 1; median time between last negative visit and first positive visit is 1.25 years)
evidence: The manuscript directly states the median time between visits.

claim: Higher SPVL is associated with significantly increased rate of transmission in serodiscordant couples.
source: This analysis revealed that higher SPVL was associated with significantly increased rate of transmission.
evidence: The manuscript reports a statistical association found in the analysis of serodiscordant couples.

claim: The best model fit for transmission rate as a function of SPVL is a stepwise function with three plateaus, where transmission rates increase from 0.019/year to 0.14/year as SPVL increases.
source: The best model fit was one where transmission rates increases from 0.019/year to 0.14/year in a stepwise fashion as SPVL increases with three plateaus (Figure 1a) (ΔAIC = −75.96 compared to null model with a fixed transmission rate, n = 817).
evidence: The manuscript reports the best-fitting model based on AIC comparison and provides specific transmission rate values.

claim: A generalised Hill function also fits the transmission rate data well (ΔAIC = -71.17 compared to the null model, n = 817).
source: A function with three steps was favoured over others, but we also show a continuous function, the generalised Hill function, that may be considered more biologically realistic (ΔAIC = - 71.17 compared to the null model, n = 817) (Figure 1a).
evidence: The manuscript reports the AIC comparison for the generalised Hill function model.

claim: Subtype A has a higher transmission rate than subtype D for all SPVL values.
source: In accordance with previous studies (Kiwanuka et al., 2009), subtype A had a higher transmission rate than subtype D for all SPVL values (Figure 3) (ΔAIC = −3.32 compared to the model without subtype, n = 817).
evidence: The manuscript reports a finding supported by data analysis and cites a previous study.

claim: Gender did not have an effect on transmission (ΔAIC = 1.66 compared to model without gender, n = 817).
source: Gender did not have an effect on transmission (ΔAIC = 1.66 compared to model without gender, n = 817)
evidence: The manuscript reports the result of model comparison showing no gender effect.

claim: Male circumcision reduced transmission both from female to male and from male to female.
source: male circumcision reduced transmission both from female to male and from male to female (ΔAIC = −3.74 for female to male, n = 321; ΔAIC = −3.17 for male to female, n = 487, compared to model without circumcision) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports the effect of circumcision on transmission with AIC comparisons.

claim: Higher SPVL is associated with significantly shorter time to AIDS.
source: We assessed the relationship between SPVL and time to AIDS from 562 incident cases with a SPVL value and information on time to AIDS, and found that higher SPVL was associated with significantly shorter time to AIDS (Figure 1c).
evidence: The manuscript reports a statistical association found in the analysis of incident cases.

claim: The best model for time to AIDS as a function of SPVL is a step function with three plateaus, with time to AIDS decreasing from 40 years to 5 years from low to high SPVL.
source: The best model was a step function with three plateaus, with time to AIDS decreasing from 40 years to 5 years from low to high SPVL (Figure 1c; ΔAIC = 137.22 compared to null model with fixed time to AIDS).
evidence: The manuscript reports the best-fitting model based on AIC comparison and provides specific time to AIDS values.

claim: The inferred gamma distribution for time to AIDS has shape parameter 1.2, similar to an exponential distribution.
source: The inferred gamma distribution had shape parameter 1.2, similar to an exponential distribution (which is the special case where shape parameter is 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports the inferred parameter value from the model fitting.

claim: Subtype D tends to confer faster disease progression, but this effect was not statistically significant in this study.
source: We found, in agreement with previous studies ( Kiwanuka et al., 2008), that subtype D tended to confer faster disease progression, but this effect was not statistically significant here (Figure 1, ΔAIC = 15.41 compared to the model without subtype, n = 562).
evidence: The manuscript reports a trend observed in the data with reference to previous studies, but notes lack of statistical significance.

claim: Time to AIDS did not significantly vary by gender (ΔAIC = 7.85 compared to the model without gender, n = 562).
source: Time to AIDS did not significantly vary by gender (Figure 1, ΔAIC = 7.85 compared to the model without gender, n = 562).
evidence: The manuscript reports the result of model comparison showing no gender effect on time to AIDS.

claim: The SPVL that maximises mean fitness is 3.4 log10 mL/copies (95% bootstrap CI [2.6; 4.0]).
source: The SPVL that maximises mean fitness is 3.4 log10 mL/copies (95% bootstrap CI [2.6; 4.0], Figure 2a).
evidence: The manuscript reports the optimal SPVL value derived from the model with confidence intervals.

claim: Prevalence of HIV in the Rakai cohort is approximately constant at 14% on average in the period 1995 to 2013.
source: Because prevalence of HIV in this cohort is approximately constant (at 14% on average in the period 1995 to 2013, Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: The manuscript reports the observed prevalence in the cohort over time.

claim: The distribution of SPVL can be closely approximated by a normal distribution.
source: Because prevalence of HIV in this cohort is approximately constant (at 14% on average in the period 1995 to 2013, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and the distribution of SPVL can be closely approximated by a normal distribution
evidence: The manuscript states that the SPVL distribution is approximately normal.

claim: Heritability of SPVL in the Rakai cohort was previously estimated at 36% (confidence interval 6–66%), using 97 donor-recipient transmission pairs.
source: heritability of SPVL in the Rakai cohort was previously estimated at 36% (confidence interval 6–66%), using 97 donor-recipient transmission pairs (Hollingsworth et al., 2010) (who are participants of the present cohort).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study that estimated heritability in the same cohort.

claim: The ODE simulations predicted a decline in mean SPVL in incident cases from 1995 to 2015, at a rate of −0.042, −0.013 and −0.0009 log10 copies/mL/year in the three scenarios chosen for within-host evolution, for a heritability of 36%.
source: The ODE simulations predicted a decline in mean SPVL in incident cases from 1995 to 2015, at a rate of −0.042, −0.013 and −0.0009 log10 copies/mL/year in the three scenarios chosen for within-host evolution, for a heritability of 36%.
evidence: The manuscript reports the predictions from the ODE model simulations.

claim: SPVL in the Rakai cohort decreased with date of seroconversion between 1995 and 2012, at a rate of −0.022 log10 copies/mL per year after adjustment for other covariates (CI [−0.04; −0.002], p=0.027, n = 603).
source: Strikingly, the data was in qualitative agreement with the evolutionary model: SPVL in the Rakai cohort decreased with date of seroconversion between 1995 and 2012, at a rate of −0.022 log10 copies/mL per year after adjustment for other covariates (CI [−0.04; −0.002], p=0.027, n = 603) (Figure 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports the observed trend in SPVL from the data analysis with statistical significance.

claim: Average SPVL in prevalent cases was declining at a rate of −0.020 log10 copies/mL.
source: Average SPVL in prevalent cases was also declining at a rate of −0.020 log10 copies/mL, although for those it is more difficult to adjust for covariates and test for significance (because the same participants are 'prevalent cases' at multiple time points) (Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: The manuscript reports the observed trend in prevalent cases.

claim: The observed trends in SPVL were best explained if mutations evolving within the host had a moderate negative impact on mean SPVL (scenario 2).
source: The observed trends were best explained if mutations evolving within the host had a moderate negative impact on mean SPVL (scenario 2).
evidence: The manuscript states which scenario best fits the observed data.

claim: SPVL decline was significant in the linear model without adjustment (−0.029 log10 copies/mL per year, CI [−0.045; −0.013], p=0.0005, n = 603).
source: SPVL decline was significant in the linear model both without adjustment (−0.029 log10 copies/mL per year, CI [−0.045; −0.013], p=0.0005, n = 603, Figure 2c)
evidence: The manuscript reports the unadjusted statistical analysis result.

claim: ART was introduced in Uganda in 2004.
source: ART was introduced in Uganda in 2004, but until 2011 ART was prescribed only at late stage infection (CD4 count below 250 cells/mL).
evidence: The manuscript states when ART became available in Uganda.

claim: Until 2011, ART was prescribed only at late stage infection (CD4 count below 250 cells/mL) in Uganda.
source: ART was introduced in Uganda in 2004, but until 2011 ART was prescribed only at late stage infection (CD4 count below 250 cells/mL).
evidence: The manuscript states the ART prescription criteria in Uganda.

claim: Improvement in micronutrient intake slows down disease progression but does not reduce plasma viral load.
source: However, improvement in nutrition would probably have no impact on the mean SPVL, as improving micronutrient intake slows down disease progression, but does not reduce plasma viral load (Fawzi et al., 2005; Friis, 2006; Baum et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies on the effect of nutrition on HIV.

claim: According to a 2006 survey in Rakai communities, households experience on average 2 months per year of food insecurity.
source: According to a survey conducted in 2006 in the Rakai communities, households experience on average 2 months per year of food insecurity, and the Household Dietary Diversity Score is 7.7 / 12 (S. Haberlen, personal communication, August 2016)
evidence: The manuscript cites a survey on food security in the study area.

claim: The Household Dietary Diversity Score in Rakai communities is 7.7 / 12, which is high enough to meet WHO dietary requirements in energy, proteins, minerals and vitamins.
source: According to a survey conducted in 2006 in the Rakai communities, households experience on average 2 months per year of food insecurity, and the Household Dietary Diversity Score is 7.7 / 12 (S. Haberlen, personal communication, August 2016), which is high enough to meet WHO dietary requirements in energy, proteins, minerals and vitamins (Steyn et al., 2006).
evidence: The manuscript cites a survey and references WHO dietary requirements.

claim: The evolutionary model predicted the observed dynamics of subtype A, D, and AD recombinants in the cohort.
source: The evolutionary model predicted the observed dynamics of subtype A, D, and AD recombinants ('R') in the cohort (Figure 3).
evidence: The manuscript states that the model predictions matched the observed data.

claim: HIV subtype A was more transmissible than subtype D for a given SPVL.
source: In particular, HIV subtype A was more transmissible than subtype D for a given SPVL (Kiwanuka et al., 2009), and therefore was predicted to increase in frequency in the population.
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study and makes a prediction based on this finding.

claim: Temporal trends in subtype frequency showed significant changes (analysis of deviance, p=0.044, n = 551).
source: This revealed significant changes in subtype frequencies (analysis of deviance, p=0.044, n = 551)
evidence: The manuscript reports the statistical test result for subtype frequency changes.

claim: Subtype A increased in frequency at a rate of 0.009 per year (bootstrap CI [−0.0007; 0.022]).
source: This revealed significant changes in subtype frequencies (analysis of deviance, p=0.044, n = 551) an increase in the frequency of subtype A (0.009 per year, bootstrap CI [−0.0007; 0.022])
evidence: The manuscript reports the rate of change in subtype A frequency with confidence intervals.

claim: Recombinants increased in frequency at a rate of 0.007 per year (CI [−0.005; 0.017]).
source: an increase in the frequency of subtype A (0.009 per year, bootstrap CI [−0.0007; 0.022]) and recombinants (0.007 per year, CI [−0.005; 0.017])
evidence: The manuscript reports the rate of change in recombinant frequency with confidence intervals.

claim: Subtype D decreased in frequency at a rate of −0.016 per year (CI [−0.027; −0.002]).
source: and a decrease in subtype D (−0.016, CI [−0.027; −0.002]), in accordance with a previous study (Conroy et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript reports the rate of change in subtype D frequency with confidence intervals and cites a previous study.

claim: The rise of subtype A and R together with the lower SPVL associated with infection with these subtypes contributes to the decline in mean SPVL at a rate of −0.003 log10 copies/mL/year.
source: The rise of subtype A and R together with the lower SPVL associated with infection with these subtypes contributes additionally to the decline in mean SPVL, but this effect is estimated at −0.003 log10 copies/mL/year, very small compared to the within-subtype evolution of SPVL at a rate of −0.022 log10 copies/mL/year (Material and methods).
evidence: The manuscript reports the calculated contribution of subtype frequency changes to SPVL decline.

claim: Within-subtype evolution of SPVL occurs at a rate of −0.022 log10 copies/mL/year.
source: The rise of subtype A and R together with the lower SPVL associated with infection with these subtypes contributes additionally to the decline in mean SPVL, but this effect is estimated at −0.003 log10 copies/mL/year, very small compared to the within-subtype evolution of SPVL at a rate of −0.022 log10 copies/mL/year (Material and methods).
evidence: The manuscript reports the rate of within-subtype SPVL evolution.

claim: SPVL declined within subtype A and D, the two major subtypes co-circulating in the region.
source: SPVL declined within subtype A and D, the two major subtypes co-circulating in the region (Figure 2d).
evidence: The manuscript reports the observed trend within each subtype.

claim: The inferred fitness functions for subtype A and D were both consistent with a decline in SPVL within each subtype.
source: The inferred fitness functions for subtype A and D were both consistent with a decline in SPVL within each subtype (Figure 3e).
evidence: The manuscript states that the model predictions are consistent with observed data.

claim: The model predicted a slower decline in SPVL within subtype A than the one observed, because this subtype is expanding in the population.
source: We note, though, that the model predicted a slower decline in SPVL within subtype A than the one observed, because this subtype is expanding in the population, which favours selection for transmission and slows down the attenuation of the virus.
evidence: The manuscript notes a discrepancy between model prediction and observation and provides an explanation.

claim: The attenuation of HIV in the Ugandan cohort is in contrast to increasing virulence in Europe.
source: The attenuation of HIV in this Ugandan cohort is in contrast to increasing virulence in Europe.
evidence: The manuscript compares the findings to trends in Europe.

claim: SPVL increased in Europe at an estimated rate of 0.013 log10 copies/mL/year over the last 28 years.
source: There, SPVL increased at an estimated rate of 0.013 (Herbeck et al., 2012) and 0.020 log10 copies/mL/year (Pantazis et al., 2014) over the last 28 years.
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies on SPVL trends in Europe.

claim: SPVL increased in Europe at an estimated rate of 0.020 log10 copies/mL/year over the last 28 years.
source: There, SPVL increased at an estimated rate of 0.013 (Herbeck et al., 2012) and 0.020 log10 copies/mL/year (Pantazis et al., 2014) over the last 28 years.
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies on SPVL trends in Europe.

claim: The European dynamics were hypothesized to result from viral adaptation to a higher optimal SPVL of 4.5 log10 copies/mL.
source: The European dynamics were hypothesized to result from viral adaptation to a higher optimal SPVL of 4.5 log10 copies/mL (Fraser et al., 2007; Herbeck et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies that proposed this hypothesis.

claim: SPVL has declined in Europe since 2004.
source: Transient selection for increased virulence could also have been important in Europe, and in fact SPVL has declined since 2004 (Pantazis et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study on recent SPVL trends in Europe.

claim: Comparison between the epidemic in Botswana and the younger epidemic in South Africa revealed declines in SPVL.
source: Our finding of HIV attenuation is consistent with another study of the evolution of HIV virulence in Africa.Comparison between the epidemic in Botswana and the younger epidemic in South Africa revealed declines in SPVL, which was hypothesized to be due to the fixation of mutations conferring adaptation to HLA variants and decreased replicative capacity (Payne et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study on SPVL trends in Africa.

claim: SPVL is probably determined by many loci of small effect.
source: Even if genomic data were available, this would be a challenging task since SPVL is probably determined by many loci of small effect (Bartha et al., 2013), and polygenic adaption is difficult to detect (Pritchard et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies on the genetic architecture of SPVL.

claim: Polygenic adaptation is difficult to detect.
source: Even if genomic data were available, this would be a challenging task since SPVL is probably determined by many loci of small effect (Bartha et al., 2013), and polygenic adaption is difficult to detect (Pritchard et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study on the challenges of detecting polygenic adaptation.

claim: Heritability of SPVL is generally around 30–40% in different settings.
source: These effects of SPVL on the viral transmission cycle, together with 30–40% viral heritability of SPVL (36% specifically in the Rakai cohort, but generally around 30–40% in different settings, [Fraser et al., 2014; Mitov and Stadler, 2016; Leventhal and Bonhoeffer, 2016]), is predicted to result in attenuation of the virus.
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies on heritability of SPVL across different settings.

claim: Reduced SPVL will contribute to reductions in onwards transmission as ART becomes more widely available.
source: As ART becomes more widely available, essentially shortening the duration of infection, reduced SPVL will contribute to reductions in onwards transmission, and so synergise with efforts to eliminate the pathogen.
evidence: The manuscript makes a prediction about the future impact of reduced SPVL.

claim: The RCCS has conducted regular surveys (approximately annual) of all consenting residents aged 15–49 in the same 50 communities since 1994.
source: The RCCS has conducted regular surveys (approximately annual) of all consenting residents aged 15–49 in the same 50 communities since 1994, collecting detailed information on demographics, sexual behaviours and health status and obtaining blood for HIV testing from all consenting participants.
evidence: The manuscript describes the study design and data collection.

claim: Virtually all HIV transmission in the Rakai population is via heterosexual vaginal intercourse.
source: Virtually all HIV transmission in this population is via heterosexual vaginal intercourse, and the rates of reported intercourse per week and month were found to be stable by HIV subtype and different study time periods.
evidence: The manuscript describes the mode of HIV transmission in the study population.

claim: The rates of reported intercourse per week and month were found to be stable by HIV subtype and different study time periods in the Rakai population.
source: Virtually all HIV transmission in this population is via heterosexual vaginal intercourse, and the rates of reported intercourse per week and month were found to be stable by HIV subtype and different study time periods.
evidence: The manuscript reports findings on sexual behavior in the study population.

claim: SPVL was defined as the mean log10 viral load for all visits occurring more than 6 months after estimated date of infection and before initiation of ART.
source: SPVL was defined as the mean log10 viral load for all visits occurring more than 6 months after estimated date of infection and before initiation of ART.
evidence: The manuscript defines how SPVL was calculated.

claim: Males had a higher SPVL than females (+0.259 log10 viral copies/mL, CI [0.14; 0.38], p=4.2 10–5, n = 603).
source: Consistent with previous studies (Farzadegan et al., 1998; Gandhi et al., 2002), males had a higher SPVL than females (+0.259 log10 viral copies/mL, CI [0.14; 0.38], p=4.2 10–5, n = 603)
evidence: The manuscript reports a statistical finding on gender differences in SPVL and cites previous studies.

claim: Subtype D conferred higher SPVL than subtype A (+0.211 relative to subtype A, CI [0.038; 0.38], p=0.017, n = 603).
source: subtype D conferred higher SPVL than other subtypes (+0.211 relative to subtype A, CI [0.038; 0.38], p=0.017, n = 603)
evidence: The manuscript reports a statistical finding on subtype differences in SPVL.

claim: Older age conferred slightly higher SPVL (+ 0.009 per year, CI [0.0008; 0.016], p=0.030, n = 603).
source: and older age conferred slightly higher SPVL (+ 0.009 per year, CI [0.0008; 0.016], p=0.030, n = 603).
evidence: The manuscript reports a statistical finding on the effect of age on SPVL.

claim: Malaria incidence is high in Uganda (50.8 episodes per 100 person years in Uganda in 2001).
source: Malaria incidence is high in Uganda (50.8 episodes per 100 person years in Uganda in 2001, [Mermin et al., 2006])
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study on malaria incidence in Uganda.

claim: Herpes simplex virus 2 (HSV-2) prevalence was roughly stable, from 70% in 1994–1998 to 88% in 2007–2008 in HIV infected individuals in the Rakai district.
source: Herpes simplex virus 2 (HSV-2) prevalence was roughly stable, from 70% in 1994–1998 (Serwadda et al., 2003) to 88% in 2007–2008 (Reynolds et al., 2012) in HIV infected individuals in the Rakai district
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies on HSV-2 prevalence in the study area.

claim: The prevalence of gonorrhea was 8.6% in 1994–1998 in the Rakai district.
source: The prevalence of gonorrhea and syphilis was 8.6% and 3.3% respectively in 1994–1998 (Ahmed et al., 2001)
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study on gonorrhea prevalence.

claim: The prevalence of syphilis was 3.3% in 1994–1998 in the Rakai district.
source: The prevalence of gonorrhea and syphilis was 8.6% and 3.3% respectively in 1994–1998 (Ahmed et al., 2001)
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study on syphilis prevalence.

claim: Coinfection by helminths is rare in most of the Rakai communities.
source: Last, coinfection by helminths is rare in most of the Rakai communities (Wawer et al., 1999)
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study on helminth prevalence.

claim: Schistosomiasis is endemic in some fishing communities living near lake Victoria, with prevalence of up to 50% in 1998–2002.
source: although schistosomiasis is endemic in some fishing communities living near lake Victoria, with prevalence of up to 50% in 1998–2002 (Kabatereine et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study on schistosomiasis prevalence.

claim: There is no evidence for an effect of helminth infection on HIV viral load.
source: However, there is no evidence for an effect of helminth infection on HIV viral load (Brown et al., 2004; Modjarrad et al., 2005; Modjarrad and Vermund, 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies on the effect of helminth infection on viral load.

claim: ART probably had little effect on the evolutionary dynamics of SPVL in Uganda because it only became available in 2004 and is initiated at relatively late stage infection.
source: ART probably had little effect on the evolutionary dynamics of SPVL in Uganda because it only became available in 2004 and is initiated at relatively late stage infection (CD4 < 250 cells/mm3 from 2004 to January 2011, and at < 350 cells/mm3 from February, 2011 to the time of writing, August 2016).
evidence: The manuscript provides reasoning based on ART availability and prescription criteria.

claim: The detailed evolutionary model of HIV SPVL evolution quantitatively reproduced the attenuation of HIV-1 virulence that happened in the last 20 years.
source: The detailed evolutionary model of HIV SPVL evolution presented here quantitatively reproduced the attenuation of HIV-1 virulence that happened in the last 20 years.
evidence: The manuscript states that the model predictions matched the observed data.

claim: The decline in virulence is predicted to continue into the future.
source: This decline in virulence is predicted to continue into the future.
evidence: The manuscript makes a prediction based on the model.

claim: Aggressive test-and-treat strategies have little predicted effect on evolutionary dynamics of SPVL.
source: This decline is unaffected by ART becoming more widely available, as even aggressive test-and-treat strategies have little predicted effect on these evolutionary dynamics (Roberts et al., 2015; Herbeck et al., 2016) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies and references a figure showing model predictions.

claim: Reduction of set-point viral loads should have resulted in a 20% reduction in incidence.
source: Reduction of set-point viral loads should have resulted in a 20% reduction in incidence, and a three years extension of untreated asymptomatic infection, increasing opportunities for timely treatment of infected individuals.
evidence: The manuscript states a prediction from the model in the abstract.

claim: Reduction of set-point viral loads should have resulted in a three years extension of untreated asymptomatic infection.
source: Reduction of set-point viral loads should have resulted in a 20% reduction in incidence, and a three years extension of untreated asymptomatic infection, increasing opportunities for timely treatment of infected individuals.
evidence: The manuscript states a prediction from the model in the abstract.

claim: Intermediate virulence maximizes pathogen fitness as a result of a trade-off between virulence and transmission.
source: Evolutionary theory hypothesizes that intermediate virulence maximizes pathogen fitness as a result of a trade-off between virulence and transmission, but empirical evidence remains scarce.
evidence: The manuscript states a theoretical hypothesis from evolutionary biology.

claim: Set-point viral load has declined in Uganda in the last 20 years.
source: Accordingly, set-point viral load, the most common measure of virulence, has declined in the last 20 years.
evidence: The manuscript states an observed trend in the abstract.

claim: Subtype A is slowly outcompeting subtype D in Uganda.
source: Our model also predicts that subtype A is slowly outcompeting subtype D, with both subtypes becoming less virulent, as observed in the data.
evidence: The manuscript states a model prediction that matches observed data in the abstract.

claim: Both subtype A and subtype D are becoming less virulent in Uganda.
source: Our model also predicts that subtype A is slowly outcompeting subtype D, with both subtypes becoming less virulent, as observed in the data.
evidence: The manuscript states a model prediction that matches observed data in the abstract.

claim: In untreated HIV infection, higher SPVL translates into higher per-contact transmission rates but also faster disease progression to AIDS and death.
source: In untreated infection, higher SPVL translates into higher per-contact transmission rates but also faster disease progression to AIDS and death.
evidence: The manuscript states a known relationship in HIV infection.

claim: An intermediate SPVL value maximises opportunities for transmission in HIV.
source: From the perspective of the transmission cycle, this creates a trade-off, under which an intermediate SPVL value maximises opportunities for transmission (Fraser et al., 2007).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study on the transmission-virulence trade-off.

claim: The transmission potential of a parasite is the product of the transmission rate and the time during which the host is alive and can transmit.
source: Indeed the transmission potential of a parasite is the product of the transmission rate and the time during which the host is alive and can transmit.
evidence: The manuscript states a theoretical concept from epidemiology.

claim: The time during which the host can transmit HIV is approximately the time to AIDS, as host death occurs shortly after the onset of AIDS.
source: The latter is approximately the time to AIDS in HIV as host death occurs shortly after the onset of AIDS and sexual activity may be reduced in the AIDS phase because of AIDS-associated symptoms (Hollingsworth et al., 2008).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study on the relationship between AIDS and transmission.

claim: Sexual activity may be reduced in the AIDS phase because of AIDS-associated symptoms.
source: The latter is approximately the time to AIDS in HIV as host death occurs shortly after the onset of AIDS and sexual activity may be reduced in the AIDS phase because of AIDS-associated symptoms (Hollingsworth et al., 2008).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study on sexual activity during AIDS.

claim: Many persons at risk of HIV infection do not routinely obtain HIV testing.
source: Since many persons at risk of infection do not routinely obtain HIV testing (Paz-Bailey et al., 2013), such changes may lead to more transmission and more newly diagnosed patients presenting with advanced infection, despite the widespread availability of antiretroviral therapy (ART).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study on HIV testing behavior.

claim: CTL escape mutations usually sweep through during infection because the fitness benefit of evading the immune system outweighs the cost of reduced replicative capacity.
source: These usually sweep through during infection because the fitness benefit of evading the immune system outweighs the cost of reduced RC that these mutations also impose (Goepfert et al., 2008; Carlson and Brumme, 2008; Matthews et al., 2008).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies on CTL escape mutations.

claim: CTL escape mutations may be reverted if the virus harbouring a costly CTL-escape mutation is transmitted to an individual where the mutation does not help evade the new host's immune system.
source: CTL escape mutations may be reverted if the virus harbouring a costly CTL-escape mutation is transmitted to an individual where the mutation does not help evade the new host's immune system (Carlson et al., 2014; Zanini et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies on reversion of CTL escape mutations.

claim: Mutations that increase the replicative capacity of the virus in all hosts may evolve within HIV.
source: Mutations that increase the replicative capacity of the virus in all hosts may also evolve (Kouyos et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study on mutations affecting replicative capacity.
